title: Prince Harry reveals a 'challenging but important' conversation that he is having with Archie and Lilibet 'fascinated' about the competitors of Invictus Games
text:
Prince Harry has revealed how he is having “challenging but important” conversations with his children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, about the competitors of the Invictus Games.
Speaking in this year’s competition held in Vancouver and Whistler, said the Duke of Sussex, 40. PEOPLE Magazine how their young children are interested in learning more about the tournament found in 2014 for military and injured women, injured and sick.
He revealed: ‘They are fascinated … It is a very interesting conversation to have with their children: explain why that person lacks a leg, why that person is missing an arm, why he looks as he does. It is challenging but important.
Harry shared how Archie, five, in particular, is “asking those questions”, adding: “As any father knows, once that door opens and ask those questions, or that conversation begins, more and more doors begin to open.
“And then start asking:” How were they injured? What is a mine? What is all this? “It becomes open Pandora’s box, to some extent, especially with children of this age, because they have no filter, and they are very curious and so inquisitive!
The Duke, who shares Archie and Lilibet, three, with his wife Meghan Markle, said he is “constantly trying” to explain what happened to the competitors and the Invictus games in an appropriate way for age.
Earl this week, Harry He proudly told Cowds how his son Archie asked to see images of ‘Grandma Diana’ walking through a mines field in Angola.
Speaking at the Invictus Games on Sunday, the Duke said that his eldest son recently expressed curiosity about the land mines, which caused a sincere conversation about the legacy of the Princess of Wales.
Prince Harry has revealed how he is having “challenging but important” conversations with his children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet (in the photo with the Duke and the Duchess of Sussex), about the competitors of Invictus Games
During an interview in a wheelchair basketball game in Vancouver, Harry told Canadian Broadcaster CTV : ‘It’s hard because children don’t always ask the right questions. There is no filter.
‘Or close it immediately, what I will never do, or participate in the conversation and try to explain things. Archie was asking about the land mines, so I was talking about how some of these types exploded (participating in the Invictus Games).
The father of two admitted that he was initially not sure how to discuss the dangers of the land mines with his little son, but found himself telling stories of those affected by them.
He continued: “I think IED (improvised explosive devices) are probably a bit at this point, but I found myself talking with him about the mines when I was five years old.”
However, what began as a discussion about land mines soon became a moving moment of reflection on Princess Diana.
“Interestingly, he gave me the opportunity to talk about my mother, his grandmother, who didn’t even really consider,” Harry explained.
Speaking in this year’s competition held in Vancouver and Whistler, the Duke of Sussex (in the photo), 40, told People magazine how his young children are eager to learn more about the tournament he founded in 2014 for Military wounded, injured and sick and women and women

‘I wanted to watch videos and photographs of her doing her thing for land mines so many years ago. He produced a very interesting conversation, different from what I thought it would be. ‘
Diana’s visit to Angola in 1997 as a guest of the International Red Cross became one of the most powerful humanitarian images of the time.
Videte of protection team, walked through a mined field on the outskirts of Huambo, highlighting the devastating impact of the land mines that remained after the brutal civil war of 20 years of Angola.
Only a few months after his tragic death in August 1997, Diana’s work contributed to a historical prohibition of land mines.
Prince Harry, who has continued his mother’s legacy, returned on his steps during a visit to Angola in 2019.
Using body armor and a protective visor, he walked along the same path in Huambo, where Diana had been photographed, now a prosperous community free of land mines.
Reflecting on that emotional moment, he said at that time: “It has been a rather emotional writing about my mother’s footsteps … see the transformation that has taken place, from an insecure and desolate place in a vibrant community.”
Now, it seems that Prince Harry is transmitting that legacy to the next generation, ensuring that Archie understands the remarkable impact of the grandmother who never knew.
